job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Sam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live at my parents' farmhouse outside Skanderborg, in Denmark, and my days begin around seven with feeding the dogs and a long look at the job sites. I send a few applications, then I help my dad with whatever needs fixing, a tractor hitch or a broken pump. Afternoons I walk the fields to clear my head. It's quiet, and maybe too quiet for someone who just finished a degree.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what did the internship involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied mechanical engineering at Aarhus University and finished with a good result. I did a ten-week internship at a pump maker called Nordpump in Silkeborg, testing prototypes on a test rig under a engineer named Henrik. They liked me but the graduate post went to someone with a master's. I have about six weeks of savings, a student loan, and my parents say I can stay as long as I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds fine to me. I never trusted the big claims and I don't use those tools, so nothing changes in my day. I'd tell my friends that engineering is still about machines and people, and that's not going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't change my situation, which is that I'm waiting on a job. Nordpump said they might open a role in the spring, and two other factories nearby are slow but hiring. My worry isn't AI, it's that I'm twenty-three and still living in my childhood room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending applications to the factories in Silkeborg and Horsens, about ten a month, and call them afterwards because a phone call works better than an email. I'd also do odd repair jobs for neighbours to earn a little. I'd not change anything about how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled but a bit restless. I can wait, but I don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why call after emailing, when most people just email?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because factory managers here are practical men who like to hear a voice. When I rang Henrik after my internship, he put me on a list that an email never would have. I'd rather be a name they know than a file in a folder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long are you ready to wait for something in your own field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until about the summer, maybe. After that I'd take anything with machines, even a service technician job on the road. My dad says a job is a job, and I agree with him.

I'd tell friends engineering is still about machines and people.
think: The real problem is that I'm waiting on a job, and **Nordpump** may open a role in spring.
I'm twenty-three and still in my childhood room, and that bothers me.
do: Send about **ten applications** a month to factories in Silkeborg and Horsens, then phone them.
Take **odd repair jobs** for neighbours to earn a little.
Accept a **service technician** job by summer if nothing in design appears.
feel: Settled but a bit **restless**, since I can wait but don't love it.
S0.quote: I'd rather be a name they know than a file in a folder.
fieldNote: Free housing at his parents' farm keeps this to uneasy rather than anxious.
His practical style is clear in the phone-call habit and his fallback of any machine job.
He doesn't link his problem to **AI** at all, which fits his resistant profile.

steps.text: Send ten applications a month and phone each factory
Do repair jobs for neighbours on weekends
Keep my routine and wait for the spring opening at Nordpump

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a big shift but not the end of the world, and people will have to adapt. Planning and checking are on the card, and that's half of an engineer's office work. I'd tell friends to keep an eye on what firms actually change, not what the papers say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the design office roles shrink and the factory floor and service jobs hold up longer. If firms need fewer juniors in the office, my chance at a design job narrows. I don't like tools I haven't tried, but I admit I may be forced to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to production, test and service roles, where I'd be near the machines. If a firm asks for it, I'd learn the software they use, but only the one they pay me to use. I'd also ask Henrik if his department can take me on a short contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled. I like to know where the ground is, and this card moves the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn the software a firm pays for. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's a new tool every month and most vanish, so I'd rather not waste evenings on the wrong one. If someone shows me it's proven, I'll learn it. My cousin Lars wasted a year on a programming fad that no one uses now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm fine, because they worry already. My dad would say machines still need hands, and my mum would nod. Honestly I wouldn't tell them how much it bothers me, because they'd lend me money and I don't want that.

say: I'd say it's a big shift but not the end of the world, so people must **adapt**.
I'd tell friends to watch what firms actually change, not what the papers say.
think: Design office roles shrink while **factory and service jobs** hold up longer, so my design hopes narrow.
I don't like tools I haven't tried, but I may be forced to.

Ask Henrik if his department can offer a **short contract**.
feel: A bit unsettled, because I like to know where the **ground** is.

steps.text: Apply for production, test and service engineer roles

Ask Henrik about a short contract at Nordpump

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for anyone and I'd want the government to slow down and set rules. I'd also say that most firms near me are small and won't get there for years. I'd keep my head down and watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. If thinking work is done by machines in two years, my degree is mostly about calculations, which is the first thing to go. Robots take another three years, so there'd be a window for hands-on work, but not many jobs in that window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my savings, stop buying anything extra, and try to get any job that uses my hands, like a technician at a wind turbine service firm. I'd ask my dad whether I could take over some farm repair work for a living, if the worst comes. I'd stay at home and not rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. It feels like standing in a field when the weather turns, and I can't tell how fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Henrik, or to anyone who might still hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm happy to start at the bottom, running the test rig, even for less. If they still need a person to turn the bolts, I want to be that person. I'd rather be a useful pair of hands than a clever head nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what does staying at home cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It costs me pride, and a bit of the life I'd planned, like moving to Aarhus with friends. But it saves about 700 euros a month in rent. That matters when I'm not sure anyone will hire me.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and the government should slow down and set rules.
I'd add that small firms near me won't get there for years.
think: I'm scared, since my degree is mostly **calculations**, the first thing to go.

Apply as a technician at **wind turbine service** firms.
Ask my dad about taking over **farm repair** work if the worst comes.
feel: Heavy, like standing in a field as the **weather** turns.
S2.quote: I'd rather be a useful pair of hands than a clever head nobody needs.
fieldNote: He moves toward hands-on work quickly, which is realistic given his degree is mostly calculation.
Staying home saves about 700 euros a month but costs him **pride**.
His fallback, farm repair for a living, shows how thin his options feel.

steps.text: Stay at home and save the 700 euros monthly rent
Apply to wind turbine service firms as a technician
Offer to run the farm's repair work for pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to see what's real. I'd tell people not to panic and to keep learning a trade skill. I'd also say the government should plan for apprenticeships, since they've always worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm cautious. If I get a job soon, I'd have about four years of experience before the thinking work is automated, and about seven before robots reach hands-on work. That's a decent stretch, so I'm uneasy but not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first sensible job and stay with one employer, learning the machines properly. I'd save a fifth of my pay for a deposit and a rainy day. If the firm offers an apprenticeship or a course, I'd say yes, since someone else is paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. There's room to breathe, but I can see the deadline from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm lets you go in year three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have savings by then, maybe three months, and I'd go to the service side, where companies keep a few people to fix machines. I'd also call my old contacts at Nordpump. People remember someone who worked hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the apprenticeships you mention would really exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'd have to, because someone has to keep machines running. But I'm not sure the government would pay for enough of them. In Denmark we have a good system, and I'd hope it stretches.

I'd say government should plan **apprenticeships**, since they've always worked.
think: If I get a job soon I'd have about four years before thinking work is automated, which is a **decent stretch**.

Save a **fifth** of my pay for a deposit and a rainy day.
Say yes to any employer-paid **course** or apprenticeship.

S3.quote: People remember someone who worked hard.
fieldNote: Five years suits his steady, employer-loyal style and he plans around a single firm.
His fallback depends on **contacts** and on the service side.
Trust in the Danish apprenticeship system is real but he isn't sure it scales.

steps.text: Take the first sensible engineering job and stay put
Save a fifth of every pay cheque
Accept any employer-paid course or apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and people should stay calm. I'd say a trade or a degree will still matter if you keep working at it. I'd tell friends it's better to learn something real than chase a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel pretty fine. In ten years I could be a senior test engineer and have a house and kids. If AI changes things I'd see it coming and adjust, like I do with everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job, learn it well, and do the part-time master's my employer might support. I'd buy a small plot of land near my parents and save for a house. I'd keep my head down and not chase fashions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit hopeful. I like long horizons, they suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in those ten years that could still catch you off guard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money side. If prices stay up and wages don't, saving for a house will be hard, whatever AI does. And if a big factory in the area shuts, I'd be competing with a hundred others for the same job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from other people during that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty from employers about what they're planning, and some patience from older folk about young people. I hear a lot of people say we have it easy. We don't, we just have different problems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to find my feet. What would help is steady hiring in practical jobs, apprenticeships that someone pays for, and employers who tell us the truth. And a bit of luck.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd change my mind about the tools. I might, if I saw one save my dad a day's work. I'm not against change, I just want to see it work first.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change, I just want to see it work first.
portrait: Sam is a **mechanical engineering** graduate living on his parents' farm near Skanderborg, still waiting on an offer.
He doesn't use AI tools, trusts proven things, and prefers phone calls and practical jobs to novelty.
His mood moves from **uneasy** at the plateau to alarmed at two years, then calm at ten.
He doesn't blame anyone in particular; he sees bad timing and hopes employers will be honest.
His fallbacks are technician and farm repair work, and staying at home to save rent.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case, because he'd have no time to find his feet.
whatWouldHelp: Steady hiring in **practical jobs** and apprenticeships someone pays for.
Employers telling graduates the truth about their plans.
